reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Typically presents as a painless, gradually enlarging anterior neck swelling that moves upward on swallowing, reflecting attachment to the thyroid cartilage
Most patients are euthyroid, but longstanding disease can develop autonomous nodules and progress to a toxic (hyperfunctioning) goitre with thyrotoxic features

Retrosternal extension may cause tracheal or oesophageal compression, producing dyspnoea, stridor, or dysphagia, and Pemberton sign (facial congestion on raising the arms) suggests thoracic inlet obstruction
Ultrasound is the first-line imaging to characterise nodules; a dominant or suspicious nodule should be sampled by fine-needle aspiration to exclude malignancy
Thyroid function tests and, where autonomy is suspected, a radionuclide uptake scan help distinguish hot (autonomous) from cold nodules
Surgical management is usually total or near-total thyroidectomy for compressive symptoms, cosmetic concern, suspected malignancy, or toxicity not controlled medically
Sudden painful enlargement of a single nodule often represents haemorrhage into a cyst rather than malignant change
reference.pathophysiology: A multinodular goitre develops through cycles of thyroid follicular hyperplasia and involution, driven by relative iodine deficiency, fluctuating TSH stimulation, and heterogeneous growth responses among follicular cells. Over time the gland becomes structurally heterogeneous, with colloid nodules, cystic degeneration, haemorrhage, fibrosis, and calcification. Some clones of cells acquire autonomous function independent of TSH, which can lead to subclinical or overt hyperthyroidism (toxic multinodular goitre). Progressive enlargement, particularly with retrosternal growth, can compress the trachea and oesophagus and displace or narrow the airway.
additionalDifferentials: Solitary thyroid nodule or thyroid adenoma
Thyroglossal cyst or other midline neck mass
additionalInvestigations: Serum TSH with free T4/T3 to define thyroid status
Neck ultrasound to map nodules and identify suspicious features
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of dominant or sonographically suspicious nodules
Radioisotope thyroid scan when autonomy or a toxic nodule is suspected
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI without iodinated contrast where feasible) for retrosternal extension and airway assessment
Flow-volume loops or laryngoscopy to assess airway and vocal cord function before surgery
redFlags: Stridor, orthopnoea, or acute airway compromise from tracheal compression
Rapid enlargement, fixation, hoarseness, or cervical lymphadenopathy suggesting malignancy
Symptoms of severe thyrotoxicosis or impending thyroid storm in a toxic goitre
Superior vena cava obstruction features from a large retrosternal goitre
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally good; benign euthyroid goitres often remain stable or are cured by thyroidectomy, and toxic goitres respond to definitive treatment. Recurrence can occur after subtotal resection, and lifelong thyroid hormone replacement is expected after total thyroidectomy.
pitfalls: Assuming all nodular goitres are benign and omitting cytology of a dominant or suspicious nodule
Overlooking retrosternal extension and airway narrowing before anaesthesia
Failing to render a toxic goitre biochemically controlled before surgery, risking perioperative thyrotoxic crisis
Not documenting preoperative vocal cord status, obscuring the cause of any postoperative hoarseness
Missing postoperative hypocalcaemia or recurrent laryngeal nerve injury after total thyroidectomy
